concepts.title: Memory as Information Processing: Stages and Stores
concepts.definition: The information-processing view treats memory as a flow: sensory memory registers input briefly, attention moves it into short-term memory where it survives seconds, and rehearsal encodes it into long-term memory's vast, durable store. Memory has a nature and stages -- encoding, storage and retrieval -- not one box.
concepts.key_idea: Three doors in sequence -- sensory, short-term, long-term -- and passage depends on attention and rehearsal.
concepts.textbook_ref: kepy106.txt stages sections (nature of memory, information processing approach, sensory register, short term memory, long term memory, encoding storage retrieval)
question_patterns: describe the stages of memory in the information processing model
in class 11 human memory: what is the capacity and duration of short term memory
how does information move from sensory to long term memory
explain encoding storage and retrieval as memory processes
why do we forget a phone number heard once
what role does attention play in memory formation

solution_steps.explain: Sensory memory holds the raw input for a fraction of a second; attention selects what proceeds.
Short-term memory keeps about seven items briefly; rehearsal maintains and deepens them.
Long-term memory stores meaningfully encoded material durably; retrieval brings it back to awareness.

concepts.title: Long-Term Memory: Types and Organisation
concepts.definition: Long-term memory splits into declarative memory -- episodic events and semantic facts that can be stated -- and procedural memory of skills that perform without words. Contents are organised in networks of associations, which is why one cue can unpack a whole episode.
concepts.key_idea: A library with wings -- episodes, facts and skills shelved in linked networks, retrievable by the right cue.
concepts.textbook_ref: kepy106.txt long term sections (declarative memory episodic semantic, procedural memory, organisation of long term memory, knowledge networks)
question_patterns: distinguish episodic and semantic memory with examples
in class 11 human memory: what is procedural memory give instances
how is long term memory organised
why does one smell recall a whole childhood scene
classify given memories as declarative or procedural
explain how knowledge networks aid retrieval

solution_steps.explain: Episodic memory files personal experiences in time; semantic memory files general facts without autobiography.
Skills -- cycling, typing -- live as procedures expressed in action, hard to put into words.
Contents link in associative networks, so a single cue activates connected memories.

concepts.title: Forgetting, and Strategies for Improving Memory
concepts.definition: Forgetting may come from trace decay, interference by older or newer material, or retrieval failure -- the material is present but the cue is missing. Memory can be strengthened by meaningful organisation, elaborative rehearsal, mnemonic devices such as the keyword method, and spaced practice.
concepts.key_idea: Forgetting is mislaid, not always erased -- better encoding and cues, spaced over time, keep memory findable.
concepts.textbook_ref: kepy106.txt forgetting sections (trace decay, interference proactive retroactive, retrieval failure, mnemonics keyword method, strategies to improve memory)
question_patterns: in class 11 human memory: distinguish proactive and retroactive interference
what mnemonics help in remembering lists
how does meaningful organisation improve memory
why does spaced practice beat cramming
suggest methods a student can use to remember better

solution_steps.explain: Check whether material faded with time, was displaced by other learning, or simply lacks a retrieval cue.
Connect new material to what you know -- elaboration and organisation build multiple retrieval routes.
Use mnemonics for lists and spread revisions over days -- consolidation beats cramming.

worked_examples.question_pattern: You hear a name at a party and forget it within a minute. Explain with the stages of memory and suggest a fix.

solution_template.explain: Without attention the name barely entered; with no rehearsal it died in short-term memory.
Sensory to short-term transfer needs attention; short-term to long-term needs rehearsal or meaning.
Repeat the name, link it to an image or a friend's name, and use it once -- encoding now reaches long-term store.

worked_examples.question_pattern: After learning physics formulas, a student finds yesterday's maths formulas confused with them. Identify the forgetting phenomenon and its type.

solution_template.explain: Old material (maths) is disturbed by new material (physics) learned later.
This backward displacement is retroactive interference.
Distinct, meaningful organisation of each subject's formulas reduces the overlap that interferes.
